content: Chiggers, also known as chigoe, refer to two distinct parasitic arthropods with similar behaviors. The first is the chigoe flea (Tunga penetrans), which is commonly found in tropical climates. The second is the larva of a harvest mite, which can carry a microscopic parasite called Orientia tsutsugamushi and is responsible for causing scrub typhus. These larvae are also referred to as scrub mites, red mites, and by other names. They are distributed across temperate and tropical regions. The term chigger originated as a variation of chigoe, but in North America, it is most commonly used to describe the harvest mite. Pathophysiology Chiggers do not burrow into the skin, nor do they feed on blood. Instead, they attach to their host and inject digestive enzymes into the bite site. These enzymes break down the host's tissue, which the chigger then consumes. Warm and rainy weather promotes the reproduction of these parasitic mites, leading to large populations. When ground temperatures consistently exceed 60°F, harvest mites begin laying eggs, marking the start of chigger season. This season typically begins in April and ends with the first frost in early autumn. Chiggers are averse to sunlight and high humidity. During wet seasons, they are commonly found in tall grass and dense vegetation. In contrast, during dry seasons, they are more likely to be located under brush or in shaded areas. Medical Treatment To alleviate the itching caused by chigger bites, it is recommended to apply an anti-itch cream containing hydrocortisone, calamine, or benzyl benzoate. If you are sensitive to these medications or have concerns, consult a healthcare professional or pharmacist for guidance. Prevention Maintain short grass in your yard. Remove brush and wood debris, as these areas can serve as habitats for potential mite hosts. Prevent rodents and other small mammals, which are common hosts for chiggers, from inhabiting the area. Secure trash cans to discourage wildlife from approaching your home. Allow sunlight to penetrate the grass, as this will dry the lawn and create an environment less conducive to chigger survival. Apply insect repellent to your feet, legs, and midsection to reduce the risk of bites. Related Topics Insect bite relief products, such as insect bite relief sticks.
